title: Quantum environment afterglow from broadband excitation spectroscopy in superconducting qubits
authors: J. R. Guimarães, Y. Liu, Y. Gao, Y. Haddad, A. Galicia, D. A. Volkov, J. T. Schmieder, H. Bhardwaj, M. Neis, J. Cereijo, M. Jerger, P. A. Bushev, R. Barends
abstract: Understanding the qubit environment is central to fault-tolerant superconducting quantum computation. Characterization typically relies on relaxation, leaving excitation largely underexplored. Here, we access this information with time-resolved broadband excitation spectroscopy. The resulting qubit excitation spectrum reveals a highly structured landscape, interspersed with cold regions. Combined with postselection, this technique enables full reconstruction of the noise power spectral density (PSD) and separates quantum from classical noise. With feed-forward, it exposes long-lived two-level-systems (TLSs), whose relaxation times span tens of microseconds to milliseconds - uncovering an intrinsic link between the qubit-TLS coupling and TLS relaxation. The data suggest that the long-lived TLSs are intrinsic to the qubit environment, and can cause excitation that lasts for many qubit operation cycles. Consequently, the environment retains a memory of prior dynamics, and properties like gate fidelity become non-Markovian and protocol-dependent. The presented approach enables identifying and bypassing the hidden roadblocks formed by long-lived TLSs in fault-tolerant quantum computation.
summary: This research introduces time-resolved broadband spectroscopy to overcome limitations in characterizing superconducting qubit environments. By probing excitation dynamics, the authors successfully reconstruct the noise spectrum and identify long-lived Two-Level Systems (TLSs). The findings demonstrate that these TLSs induce non-Markovian noise, presenting a critical roadblock for achieving fault-tolerant quantum computation.
main_problem: Characterizing the quantum environment of superconducting qubits is crucial for fault-tolerant computation, but traditional methods fail to fully explore the excitation dynamics.
main_result: The study reveals that long-lived Two-Level Systems (TLSs) are intrinsic to the environment, causing non-Markovian dynamics that can limit gate fidelity and require new characterization techniques.
method: The authors employ time-resolved broadband excitation spectroscopy, combined with postselection and feed-forward, to reconstruct the full noise power spectral density and probe environmental memory effects.
model_or_system: The system is a frequency-tunable transmon superconducting qubit coupled to an environment containing intrinsic noise sources, primarily TLSs. The analysis uses master equations and time-dependent population measurements to model the qubit-TLS interaction.
key_observables: Qubit excitation spectrum, full noise power spectral density (PSD), effective temperature ($T_{eff}$), and environmental memory time ($T_{1,Env}$).
important_parameters: TLS relaxation times spanning microseconds to milliseconds; coupling strength ($g_{q-TLS}$); non-Markovianity.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the ability to separate environmental contributions from intrinsic qubit decay, and that the coupling strength is sufficient to populate TLSs for detection.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the setup, the decomposition of total noise PSD into classical and quantum components, and time-dependent measurements ($\Delta P_1$ vs $\Delta t$) used to distinguish Markovian from non-Markovian environmental coupling.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from identifying the limitation of standard relaxation measurements to introducing broadband spectroscopy. It then details the analysis to separate noise sources, quantify the impact of long-lived TLSs, and concludes by proposing methods to bypass these environmental roadblocks.
why_interesting: This work provides a detailed, experimental roadmap for characterizing non-Markovian noise sources in superconducting qubits, directly impacting the feasibility and error budgeting for quantum computation architectures.
